planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in a sheltered site with morning sun and afternoon shade, in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil.

directions: This Chinese mountain bamboo earns its common name from culms that shed their outer layer to reveal a smooth, papery, cinnamon-toned surface rather than the usual green or waxy bloom. It forms a tight, non-invasive clump and tolerates a surprising range of light from open shade to filtered sun, though foliage stays greener and less stressed with afternoon protection in hot regions. Give it room to mature into a tall screening clump over several seasons, since young plants are slow to show their eventual height. Protect from drying wind, which can scorch the thin, papery culm surface before it hardens.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in cool-summer climates with morning sun and afternoon shade, allowing generous room for one of the largest temperate clumping bamboos.

directions: Among the fastest-growing and largest of the cold-hardy clumping bamboos, this Sichuan native sends up new shoots with a distinctive pale blue cast before the feathery, arching foliage matures to green. It is considered one of the most cold-tolerant Borinda species, but it is fundamentally a shade-loving plant and struggles with scorch, yellowing, or stunted growth where summers are intensely hot or humid. Clumps spread a bit more loosely than typical Fargesia, so plan for a wide planting area rather than a tight specimen bed. It performs best in the mild, cool-summer climates of the Pacific coast and similar maritime regions.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring behind a rhizome barrier in dappled shade and moist, humus-rich soil for a lush low screen or groundcover.

directions: This running bamboo is grown almost entirely for its leaves, which reach up to a foot long and two inches wide, the largest of any commonly cultivated hardy bamboo. It thrives in dappled or partial shade where its oversized, deep-green foliage can form a dense, low privacy screen or textural groundcover beneath trees. Because it spreads by rhizomes, install a barrier at planting time unless you intend to let it colonize a naturalized shade bed. It holds up well in wind and tolerates average garden soil as long as moisture is consistent through the growing season.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in partial shade in well-drained soil; this South African highland bamboo tolerates drier summers better than most clumping species.

directions: Native to the south-eastern highlands of South Africa and Lesotho, this clumping bamboo is unusual for having canes that are notably thick in proportion to its modest height, giving it a stout, sturdy look rather than the willowy habit typical of mountain bamboos. Persistent creamy-white culm sheaths and a bluish waxy bloom give young canes a frosted appearance, while mature culms blush purple where they catch strong light. It is more tolerant of heat and drier conditions than most Fargesia-type bamboos, making it a useful clumping option for Mediterranean-climate or dry-summer shade gardens. Its dense, upright clumps work well as a specimen or a tall informal screen.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring where it gets morning sun and afternoon shade, in moist but well-drained soil; this high-elevation Himalayan species needs consistent moisture to settle in.

directions: Known locally in its native Himalayan range as dev-ringal, this clump-forming bamboo grows naturally as understory cover in subalpine forests from northern India to Bhutan, which suits it well to shaded or dappled garden settings. Smooth, glaucous-green young culms mature to yellow or reddish brown, and the dense root mass has enough soil-binding strength that it has traditionally been used to stabilize slopes. It prefers morning sun with afternoon shade in regions with hot summers, and once established needs comparatively little maintenance. Use it as a specimen clump, informal hedge, or screen in a woodland-edge planting.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring behind a rhizome barrier in part to full shade as a low groundcover or lawn substitute in moist, well-drained soil.

directions: This low, running bamboo is grown for its thick, dark-green leaves striped with cream to white variegation, forming one of the more eye-catching groundcovers available in shade gardens. It stays under two feet tall and spreads steadily by rhizomes, tolerating mowing or shearing in early spring, which actually encourages fresh, more strongly variegated foliage for the season. It handles everything from dense shade to brighter spots but colors up best and looks least stressed out of hot direct sun. Because it spreads readily, confine it with a barrier or use it intentionally as a spreading lawn alternative under trees.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring behind a rhizome barrier in half-sun to shade in consistently moist, well-drained soil.

directions: This selection of a South-Central Chinese species is grown as a shrub-scale running bamboo, valued for broad, relatively large lanceolate leaves and the swollen, knuckle-like nodes typical of its genus. It is a shade-loving bamboo by nature and performs best with half-day sun or filtered light rather than full exposure, especially where summers run hot. Moderately cold-hardy once dormant, it still benefits from a sheltered spot at the cooler edge of its range. Like other Chimonobambusa, it spreads by running rhizomes, so a barrier is recommended to keep it within an intended planting area.
